note: Build a blend-oriented backbone that captures most feed value with five columns before deciding whether heavy separations pay.
notebook:

Initial five-column design targets ethane, C3 mix, C4 mix, C5 mix and C6 paraffin mix. Heavies remain unsold initially. Moderate 35-50 stages and R=B=3 limit expensive-plant cost; 0.1 pressure drop avoids extreme operating pressures.

note: Focus on three sharp blend splits and remove nonproductive branches; higher reflux should eliminate the heavy leakage that made every product unsellable.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 establish a profitable blend-oriented skeleton: sharp C4-/C5+ split, then C3/C4 and C5/C6+ splits. Step 2 tune costly columns and add C6/heavy recovery only where marginal value exceeds cost.
Turn 1 showed all C4- report to root tops but 27% of C5 leaks upward; downstream splits similarly too sloppy at R=3. The immediate priority is three saleable blend streams, not the costly C6-paraffin/naphthene split. Removed TT and BB, raised root/T/B separation, and lowered pressure to dp=0.3 (peer root was cheaper at dp=0.3). Target C4 mix (~$185M/yr) and C5 mix (~$575M/yr); C3 is upside if T tops meets spec.

note: Shift all three cuts downward by reducing boil-up, aiming to keep C5 out of the C4 product and C6 out of the C5 product without adding columns.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 establish a profitable blend-oriented skeleton: sharp C4-/C5+ split, then C3-waste/C4 and C5/C6+ splits. Step 2 tune costly columns and add C6/heavy recovery only where marginal value exceeds cost.
Current cuts are close in flow but too much C5 rises at the root and too much C6 rises in B. All three columns have excess overhead flow, so reduce boil-up from 3 to 2 while retaining high reflux/stages. TT cannot qualify as C3 mix because ethane alone is 10%; treat it as waste and prioritize C4 ($180M/yr) plus C5 ($564M/yr). Avoid extra columns until these two revenues appear.

note: Move the root cut upward just enough to recover the C4 lost to the bottoms, and drive residual C3 overhead in T; this should unlock both C4 and C5 blend sales.
notebook:
PLAN: Step 1 establish a profitable blend-oriented skeleton: sharp C4-/C5+ split, then C3-waste/C4 and C5/C6+ splits. Step 2 tune costly columns and add C6/heavy recovery only where marginal value exceeds cost.
At boil-up 2.0 root tops were only 699 versus 864 mol/s C4-and-lighter, leaving ~165 C4 in B; this contaminated BT and prevented both C4 and C5 sales. Increase root boil-up modestly to 2.4 rather than 3.0 (which previously drove C5 overhead). T bottoms contained ~139 C3, so raise its boil-up to 3.0 to reject ethane/C3 overhead while retaining C4. Keep B unchanged initially because correcting the root should make its existing cut close to the 695 mol/s C5 blend. TT is waste unless later purified; C4 and C5 are the first revenue targets.

note: Copy the island’s profitable C6-paraffin backbone and add one clean C4/C5 split to monetize its large C5 content.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt the profitable R170 C6-paraffin backbone, recover the valuable C5 blend from its unsold light tops, then test a C3/C4 splitter and finally reduce column costs without losing product specifications.
R170 earns $941.9M/yr from a clean C6 paraffin cut using two columns and scores 0.728. Its root tops are nearly exactly all C5-and-lighter material (1562 mol/s), so a single C4/C5 splitter should yield about 695 mol/s of C5 blend worth roughly $560M/yr. Start with 55 stages, reflux 4.5 and boil-up 2.0: the clean feed should make this much easier than my previous contaminated C5 split. Preserve R170 root and B settings exactly. The remaining light overhead can later yield C4 mix (~$164M/yr), while ethane/C3 purification is likely uneconomic.

note: Raise the C4/C5 splitter boil-up sharply: prior results show this drives n-butane overhead, and reaching the valuable C5 blend specification should dominate the extra energy cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt the profitable R170 C6-paraffin backbone, recover the valuable C5 blend from its unsold light tops, then test a C3/C4 splitter and finally reduce column costs without losing product specifications.
Step 1: sharpen the C4/C5 split. My boil-up 2.0 sent far too much C4 into TB (34% n-butane). R218 and R214 show that raising boil-up to 3.5/5.0 reduces C4 leakage to 21%/15%, so try 7.0 while retaining the moderate 55 stages and reflux 4.5. A clean C5 blend is worth roughly $560M/yr, easily justifying additional duty. Preserve R170 root and B exactly. If C5 sells, optimize this splitter’s cost and consider C4 recovery from TT.

note: Adopt R262’s proven four-column design and sharpen the inexpensive C3/C4 splitter to seek 99% premium n-butane rather than 96% standard grade.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt R262’s profitable C4/C5 recovery, upgrade its n-butane column toward 99% premium purity, then test whether ethane removal can profitably unlock the C3 blend and finally trim expensive backbone duties.
Step 2: R262 adds a cheap 45-stage TT column and earns $151M/yr from 96% n-butane, raising reward to 1.982. Its TTB still contains 4% isobutane; a sharper 60-stage, reflux-6 split should reduce isobutane leakage and may reach the 99% premium threshold, adding about $48M/yr for modest extra cost. T reflux 5.0 also improves C5 recovery over my current 4.5. Preserve root and B. Next, if TTB remains saleable, consider a small TTT ethane/C3 splitter; otherwise optimize TT settings.

note: Restore the proven inexpensive C4 cut and trim the oversized heavy splitter, which has purity margin and the second-largest column cost.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore R262’s best four-column settings, then reduce the costly heavy-column size/reflux while preserving its 98% C6-paraffin product; afterward trim root/T duties and only add separations with clear value.
Step 3: My 60-stage/reflux-6 TT was counterproductive: TTB fell to 91% n-butane because more feed reported bottoms, giving only $167M versus R262’s $151M but at $23M extra cost; net reward 1.966. R262 at TT 45/4/5 gives reward 1.982. B has 2% naphthene leakage and $249M cost, so test 70 stages/reflux 6 instead of 80/7. R309’s extra C3 split and R311’s heavy splitters both destroyed value; avoid those branches.

note: Use the remaining C6-paraffin purity margin to reduce the heavy splitter’s stages and reflux while holding its successful cut.
notebook:
PLAN: Trim the proven four-column plant in order of cost: B first, then root and T, retaining blend purity. Add no heavy/light branches unless a trim creates a clearly valuable opportunity.
Step 4: Best is 2.151 with B 70/6/5. BT has 97% C6 paraffins (3% methylcyclopentane), so there is purity margin below the 95% blend threshold. Test B 60/5/5; R359/R357 show extra heavy splitters cost more than they earn, and extra C3 splitting also failed. Root ($373M) and T ($169M) are next targets.

note: Adopt the profitable octane-producing heavy branch and trim the dominant root column; the cut and pressure stay fixed to isolate whether its size and reflux have margin.

Step 1: R402 earns 2.269 by adding BB/BBB/BBBB for $243.5M octane revenue at $191.9M extra cost. B cannot be cut to 60/5: C6 blend falls just below 95% and loses $1002M. Root is the largest cost ($373.3M), so test 55/4.5/6 at the same successful cut and pressure. Watch TB and BT purity plus octane recovery.

note: Use the island-best heavy train and raise final-column boil-up to recover some of the 99 mol/s octane currently stranded in BBBBB, exploiting the existing purity margin.
notebook:
PLAN: Start from island-best R453 (2.603), improve octane recovery in its final inexpensive column, then test cautious backbone cost reductions only if product purity remains robust.
R453 sells C5/C6 blends, 96% n-butane, 99% heptane and 98% octane. Its BBBB feed contains about 233 mol/s octane but only 137 is sold; 99 remains in worthless bottoms. There is 1% purity headroom before standard grade is lost, so raise BBBB boil-up 7->8 at fixed 60 stages/reflux 8. This should recover more octane overhead for little extra cost. Root 55/4.5 failed badly by leaking DMB into C5; do not repeat aggressive backbone trims.

note: Push the proven octane/nonane splitter to stronger stripping: at boil-up 15 the bottoms still hold 41% octane, leaving both nonane and substantial octane value stranded.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt R505's best 2.730 plant, finish the octane/nonane split by raising final stripping, then evaluate low-risk cost trims in oversized backbone columns.
R505 at BBBB boil-up 15 sells 193 mol/s 99% octane, but its bottoms still contain 44 mol/s octane and only 59% nonane. Nonane is worth $104M/yr and remaining octane about $80M/yr, so further stripping can unlock roughly $180M/yr gross. Increase boil-up 15->25 while retaining validated 60 stages/reflux 8; target >95% nonane bottoms and near-complete octane overhead. R503 boil-up12 and my boil-up8 establish monotonic recovery. Avoid backbone trims: root 55/4.5 previously destroyed C5 purity.

note: Add R554’s inexpensive nonane polisher below my stronger octane stripper; its feed is already 84% nonane, so this should monetize nonane while retaining the extra octane recovery.
notebook:
PLAN: Combine my stronger octane stripping with R554’s compact nonane polisher, then use remaining solves for one or two high-value cost or recovery improvements.
My BBBB boil-up25 yields 224 mol/s 99% octane and leaves only 74 mol/s bottoms (84% nonane), versus boil-up15 leaving 106 mol/s. R554’s 45/4/6 polisher on that larger, less pure bottoms makes 100% nonane for only $19.6M/yr. Applying the same polisher to my 84%-nonane stream should recover nearly all 62 mol/s feed nonane (~$104M/yr gross) at lower cost, while preserving my extra $49M/yr octane. If successful this should clearly exceed R554’s 2.897. Avoid root double effect: R552 lost heat integration and destroyed product cuts.

notebook:
PLAN: Adopt R601’s dual-sale heavy tail, then apply the two independently demonstrated cost trims (BBBB reflux 4 and compact T) while retaining its strong final polisher; next optimize the largest splitters only if purity remains secure.
R601 scores 3.102 by using a 60/8/6 polisher: its 45 mol/s overhead is 97% octane ($66.6M) and bottoms are premium nonane ($122.3M). R598 proves BBBB reflux 4 still gives 99% octane overhead and saves $34.5M/yr; its leaner 69 mol/s bottoms are 90% nonane. R602 proves T=45/4/6 retains saleable C5 and 95% butane while saving about $20M/yr net. Combining these with R601’s polisher should preserve nonane and move most octane recovery into the cheaper BBBB column. Avoid double effects and avoid adding the marginal BBT train.

notebook:
PLAN: Start from island-best R649 (naphthene recovery), then monetize the stranded C3-rich TTT with one easy C3/C4 split. If profitable, test disciplined trims on the very expensive root/B columns while protecting all blend specifications.

TTT is 442 mol/s containing essentially all ethane, propylene and propane plus C4s. A 45-stage reflux-4 splitter should make a clean ~320 mol/s C3-blend overhead worth about $70M/yr; its C4-rich bottoms need not sell. Prior lessons: BBBB reflux 4 preserves premium octane and saves $34.5M; final polisher is worthwhile; avoid speculative heavy-train additions beyond the proven naphthene pair.

notebook:

BBB has a very sharp heptane/octane cut and 99% product, so 45 stages/reflux 5 may retain premium quality. BBTB overhead is 98% naphthene-blend members, giving some purity margin for 45 stages/reflux 5/boil-up 5. R695 showed stronger BBTB duties are counterproductive. Preserve BBBB=60/4/15 and BBBBB=60/8/6, which monetize octane and nonane profitably.
